So it all depends on the VIN number. There are some batches of engines from 2009 that are complete crap. Other than that, they're solid cars. Watch out for more common boxer engine problems that are a real pain to fix like leaky valve cover gaskets. I've listed the major differences between the years so you have some more info.

2008 - first year for this gen 2009 - 265 HP + suspension changes 2010 - added bluetooth ( later in the year), suspension changes, minor other tweaks 2011 - added wide body kit, wheel size change, suspension changes = wider track 2012 - changed nav unit and headlights, added PBP as a color choice

Good luck. I have no doubt that you'll immediately fall in love. Feel free to ask more questions here and consider joining NASIOC.

I think a new shortblock goes for around $2000. That being said, if you find one for a reasonable price and you've got the cash, have fun with it! I worry about mine, but it is totally worth it to me.

Ingredients:

  • 1 tablespoon margarine spread (such as Smart Balance)
  • ½ teaspoon cinnamon
  • 2 tablespoons artificial brown sugar blend (such as Splenda)
  • 2 medium pears, cored and sliced in half
  • 1 tablespoon chopped walnuts
  • ¼ cup water

Instructions:

  1. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees.
  2. In a small bowl combine margarine, cinnamon and brown sugar. Add walnuts and mix.
  3. Arrange the pears cut side up in an 8-inch square glass baking dish. Pour ¼ cup water in bottom of pan.
  4. Divide the brown sugar mixture evenly among the pear halves and place in middle of pears.
  5. Bake until the pears are tender and beginning to brown, about 45 minutes.

Nutrition Information per Serving (1/2 Pear):

  • Calories 100
  • Carbohydrates 19 g
  • Protein 1 g
  • Fat 3.5 g
  • Dietary Fiber 3 g
  • Sodium 25 mg

Hey! IAMA 30+ year veteran server of restaurants of all shapes and colors. Something you want to know about the server experience? Insider info on restaurants in general? Ask me anything!

That largely depends on the P.O.S. system (point of service) the particular restaurant uses. Some have excellent features for modifying orders and then again some are a total nightmare. Whichever, good servers know how to communicate with kitchen to get the order properly prepared for the guest.
Another question, what is your view on the American culture of tipping?

I love making tips. It gives me a lot of control over my income. I treat my section as if it were my own business. Good service generally = good tips. Of course this is always subjective. Some people hate the idea of the tipping culture, but honestly, I find most guests are generous and thankful for good service.

Thanks for the AMA!

What do you think of the NYC restaurant that upped wages, but eliminated tipping and their business and profitability increased?

I'll try to answer this the best I can. I worked in a restaurant once that had a very diverse reservation list. Small parties and business related reservations that were larger parties. It could be rather difficult to distribute the sections in a way that could fairly accommodate opportunities equally for servers to make money. There was some grumbling of servers that got a lesser advantage to earn tips. I suggested to the owner that we pool the tips equally amongst the servers on shift that night so that everyone got an equal share of the pie. Nobody liked that idea at all, but the owner was open-minded and decided we should give it a try. So for a few weeks we shared tips equally based on the entire night's taking. At first servers didn't quite understand why they should share tips with some other server that did less sales. What eventually happened is that this system created a cohesiveness of service because every server benefited by the overall success of the whole. We all grew to like it. I kind of see this as a similar situation.

How do Chefs like it when the customer just asks for "something good" and leaves it to the chef's discretion? I always thought of it as a complement, but I've heard that it's not really appreciated in the kitchen.

That really kinda depends on 2 things: #1. Is it crunch time? Think of chefs in terms of rush hour traffic. The chefs are the road and you, the guest, are the traffic. We all want to get where we're going, but the shear volume of traffic limits the capabilities of the road. Now your special request can be like a car accident in the 2nd lane of a freeway. In restaurant terms we call this a "show stopper". Excellent chefs try their best to honor requests but they are not going to dig it in the heat of battle. They are pumping out orders as fast as they can and you are a "show stopper". They hate you guaranteed. #2 Is this an actual, creative, talented, chef? Hell yes!! Any, "how to get a job in a restaurant" tips? All in all do you consider it a profession worthwhile to make into a livelihood? I'm in my thirties now and have a job, but all the times I've tried over the years always ended in failure. I've always thought it would have been a fun career.

Having a resume showing experience def. helps. The interview is key. Expressing enthusiasm for service is a biggie. If you don't have experience, then, like anything else, you have to start off small. You will not likely get hired at a fine dining establishment. There is a ton to know before you can execute excellent service. You can make as much money as you want, providing you are willing to learn put in the hours and give an actual fuck about your guests.
Does the kitchen mess with food that comes back as undercooked, over seasoned, under seasoned, etc. as revenge? I never say or send anything back just because of this.

The kitchen staff takes it personal. I've def. seen cunty behavior from chefs that are butthurt by returned food. Sometimes it's justified. Often it's not. Food is very personal to peeps. Guests often expect food exactly as their mother prepared for them. That's not a realistic expectation. I will tell you however, they mostly care about your satisfaction and usually will acknowledge and correct their shortcomings. The heart of the house is the kitchen and the gears of that machine runs almost constantly. You're in your car at a stop light. Your not moving, but that engine is still cranking. Servers are the chrome and the paint job. We shine it up and try our best to make it look pretty, but if the engine is running rough, we'll give it the oil.
